definitions.definition: The eighth, fundamental consciousness: the maturation of past action, which holds all seeds, appropriates the body, cognizes the receptacle world imperceptibly, is accompanied only by the five universal mental factors and neutral feeling, flows like a torrent, and ceases (as ālaya) at arhatship.

cross_language.form: kun gzhi rnam par shes pa

equivalents.note: The Mahāyānasaṃgraha (ch. 1) says the ālaya was taught by other schools under other names — the Sthaviras' bhavaṅga-vijñāna among them; the Theravāda does not accept a store of seeds.
The Laṅkāvatāra relates ālaya and tathāgatagarbha; Faxiang keeps them distinct (the ālaya is defiled and ceases), Dilun/Shelun and Tathāgatagarbha readers identify its pure aspect with suchness.

definitions.definition: A name of the store-consciousness as that which appropriates and sustains the body and the seeds; the Saṃdhinirmocana says it is deep and subtle and was not taught to the childish lest they take it for a self.

cross_language.form: len pa'i rnam par shes pa

definitions.definition: The store-consciousness considered as the result of past action; the first of the three transformations of consciousness.

cross_language.form: rnam par smin pa'i rnam shes

definitions.definition: The store-consciousness as the root in which the five sense-consciousnesses arise like waves in water.

The seventh consciousness, called 'mind' (manas), whose nature is thinking; it depends on and takes as object the store-consciousness, grasping it as a self, and is always accompanied by four afflictions — self-view, self-delusion, self-conceit and self-love; absent in the arhat, in the attainment of cessation and on the supramundane path.

cross_language.form: nyon mongs pa can gyi yid

definitions.definition: In Yogācāra, specifically the seventh consciousness (kliṣṭa-manas) that thinks of the ālaya as 'I'; in the triad citta–manas–vijñāna, citta is the store, manas the self-grasping mentation, vijñāna the six operative cognitions.

The sixth consciousness, cognizing mental objects; it arises always except in the heaven of non-perception, the two mindless attainments, deep sleep and fainting; it is the one that conceptualizes and is first transformed (into discerning wisdom) on the path.

cross_language.form: yid kyi rnam par shes pa

definitions.definition: The consciousnesses that arise from the store as waves from the ocean: the six object-cognitions (and, in the Trisvabhāvanirdeśa's sevenfold count, the afflicted mind).

Explained (Trisvabhāvanirdeśa 7) as twofold: the store, called citta because it is 'accumulated' (cita) with seeds of defilement, and the operative mind, called citta because it arises with 'variegated' (citra) images; in the triad citta–manas–vijñāna it is the ālaya.
Any momentary cognition, which is reflexively aware of itself; mind arises from a previous moment of mind, not from the body alone.

A factor that arises associated with a consciousness and apprehends the particular features of its object, while consciousness apprehends the object itself; the Triṃśikā lists universal, particular, wholesome, afflicted, secondary-afflicted and variable factors (fifty-one in the later count).
The five factors present in every mind: contact, attention, feeling, perception and volition; the only ones that accompany the store-consciousness.

The derivative afflictions (anger, enmity, concealment, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, dishonesty, pride, harmfulness, shamelessness, non-embarrassment, torpor, agitation, lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, non-awareness) listed in the Triṃśikā.

The six root afflictions — greed, aversion, delusion, conceit, (wrong) views and doubt — which with their secondary afflictions constitute the afflictive obscuration; the afflicted mind has its own four afflictions of self.

The process in which consciousness changes and appears as self and dharmas; threefold as maturation (the store), mentation (the afflicted mind) and object-cognition (the six); all figurative talk of self and dharmas refers to it, and it is itself 'imagination'.
The thesis that the three realms are nothing but cognition: what appears as external objects is cognition appearing as objects, as in a dream or an eye-disease.
Both the thesis 'everything is cognition-only' and, in its final sense, the perfected nature itself: suchness, in which consciousness abides when it no longer apprehends an object (Triṃśikā 25, 28).

Mind-only: the teaching (Daśabhūmika, Laṅkāvatāra) that the three realms are only mind; used as a synonym of cognition-only, and in the meditative sequence the stage in which the yogin sees objects as mind before abandoning even mind as an object.

notes: In Tibetan doxography 'Cittamātra' (sems tsam pa) names the Yogācāra school as a tenet system.

definitions.definition: A potency deposited in the store-consciousness by experience and action, which later ripens as a moment of consciousness or its object; seeds are momentary, simultaneous with their fruit, continuous as a series, morally determinate, dependent on conditions and productive of their own fruit (Mahāyānasaṃgraha); Dharmapāla holds that some are innate and some newly perfumed.

The impression left in the store-consciousness by action and by the twofold grasping, which produces the next maturation (rebirth) when the former is exhausted; imprints of names, of self-view and of the factors of existence.
The beginningless imprint of conceptual thinking that makes cognition appear divided into grasped and grasper and makes universals seem real.

equivalents.note: Yoga Sūtra 4.8–9 and Yogācāra both speak of latent impressions (saṃskāra / vāsanā) that ripen; Yogācāra lodges them in the ālaya, Yoga in the citta of an unchanging puruṣa's world.

definitions.definition: The dormant tendency of the twofold grasping, which does not cease as long as consciousness does not abide in cognition-only.
Grasping at object (grāhya) and subject (grāhaka); its imprints together with those of action drive rebirth, and its latent tendency is removed only when cognition-only is realized.
The duality of object and subject, which does not exist in unreal imagination though it appears there.
The appearance of cognition as divided into object, subject and awareness, seen by those whose vision is distorted, although cognition itself is undivided.
The pair grasped–grasper, which is absent from unreal imagination; the perfected nature is the absence of duality.

The dependent nature as the mind and mental factors of the three realms: it exists, while the duality it projects does not; it is 'unreal' because its objects are unreal, but it is not wholly non-existent, and its extinction is liberation.

cross_language.form: yang dag pa ma yin pa'i kun rtog

definitions.definition: The transformation of consciousness as such, which constructs what it imagines; what is imagined does not exist.
Conceptual cognition, based on names, whose object is a universal and which is not perception; known by each in his own experience.
The way consciousness arises appearing as objects, beings, self and cognitions, although its object does not exist.

The mental image that is the object of meditative calm and insight; the Saṃdhinirmocana teaches that it is not different from the mind; the Śrāvakabhūmi distinguishes images with and without conceptualization.
The imagined, dependent and perfected natures under which every dharma is to be understood: how it appears, what appears, and the absence of the appearing duality.

cross_language.form: rang bzhin gsum; mtshan nyid gsum

definitions.definition: Whatever is imagined by any imagination — objects as external, the duality of grasped and grasper, the own-being posited by names; it does not exist at all ('natureless by its very characteristic').

cross_language.form: 遍計所執性 bianji suozhi xing

definitions.definition: Imagination itself, arising from conditions — unreal imagination; it exists, but not as it appears; it is the basis of both defilement and purification.
The dependent's constant absence of the imagined — emptiness, suchness, cognition-only-ness; neither other nor not other than the dependent; the ultimate of dharmas.

cross_language.form: 圓成實性 yuancheng shi xing

equivalents.note: Triṃśikā 25 identifies the perfected nature with suchness.

definitions.definition: The threefold naturelessness intended by the Prajñāpāramitā's 'all dharmas are without own-nature': of characteristic (the imagined), of arising (the dependent, which does not arise by itself) and ultimate (the perfected, which is naturelessness itself).
The imagined nature's naturelessness: it has no characteristic of its own, like a flower in the sky.
The dependent nature's naturelessness: it does not arise by itself but only from conditions, like a magical illusion.
The perfected nature as the ultimate, which is the very absence of own-nature (of the imagined), like space.
The perfected nature, so called because it is always thus; the ultimate of dharmas and cognition-only-ness; undifferentiated in all beings and, when purified, tathāgatahood.

literal: the element of dharmas; the sphere of reality

definitions.definition: A synonym of emptiness, so called because it is the cause of the noble dharmas; directly perceived when mind-only is itself abandoned; in its purity it is the buddhas' body operating as the three bodies.
The non-existence of duality and the existence of that non-existence, present within unreal imagination; neither defiled nor undefiled because mind is luminous; the emptiness of person and dharmas.
Seeing emptiness (selflessness) is what liberates; the other contemplations serve it.
Synonym of emptiness, meaning the non-erroneous.
Synonym of emptiness, meaning the cessation of signs.
The perfected nature as the highest object; neither existent nor non-existent, neither arising nor ceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, not purified yet purified.
Suchness without the division of grasped and grasper, which is nirvāṇa, as distinct from dharmas — the appearance of duality and names, which is saṃsāra (Dharmadharmatāvibhāga).
Metaphorical use of words; all talk of self and dharmas is figurative, referring to transformations of consciousness.

The illusion of an elephant conjured from a piece of wood by a spell, the simile of the three natures: the elephant is the imagined, its shape the dependent, the elephant's absence the perfected; the spell is the root consciousness, the wood suchness.
The simile of Viṃśatikā 1: as one with an eye-disease sees non-existent hairs, so non-existent objects appear to cognition.
The chief example of cognition-only: in dreams objects appear in determinate places and times and have effects, yet do not exist; the unawakened do not know this.
Beings who, by shared karma, all see a river of pus where others see water — the Viṃśatikā's example of intersubjective agreement without external objects.
The Viṃśatikā's example: hell-guardians are seen by all the damned and torment them, though they are not beings but transformations of the damned's own consciousness produced by their karma.
The supposed indivisible unit of matter, refuted: an atom joined on six sides would have six parts; without parts atoms could not aggregate, cast shadow or obstruct.
Mental action, declared by the Buddha the most blameworthy of the three kinds of action — as the sages' anger emptied the Daṇḍaka forest — used to show that mind acts directly on mind.
The special intention with which the Buddha taught the sense-fields as existent, for the sake of those to be trained — a key hermeneutical term.
The absence of a self in the person, entered through the teaching of the aggregates, bases and elements; knowing it removes the afflictive obscuration.
The absence of an imagined own-nature in dharmas themselves, entered through the teaching of cognition-only; knowing it removes the cognitive obscuration.
The obscuration consisting of the afflictions, which prevents liberation; removed by knowledge of the selflessness of persons.

literal: cognitive obscuration; obscuration of the knowable

definitions.definition: The subtler obscuration that prevents omniscience, removed by knowledge of the selflessness of dharmas; a buddha alone is free of both obscurations.

The heaviness or unworkability of body and mind, the latent substrate of defilement; its twofold removal (afflictive and cognitive) is the transformation of the basis; pliancy removes it in meditation.

The disposition to awakening in one of the vehicles, described as a seed, element or nature: naturally present (a distinctive feature of the six bases, beginningless) or developed (by cultivating roots of good); beings are of the disciples', solitary buddhas', bodhisattvas' or undetermined lineage, and some are without lineage.
The condition of beings who lack the lineage for liberation — the fifth of the five lineages; the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra distinguishes those temporarily cut off from those lacking the cause altogether.
The lineage that is a beginningless distinctive feature of a bodhisattva's six sense-bases, obtained by the nature of things.
The lineage obtained by prior cultivation of roots of good.

In the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, the statement that all embodied beings 'have it as their embryo' because suchness, undifferentiated in all, is tathāgatahood when purified — held alongside the doctrine of differing lineages.

The turning of the basis — the store-consciousness, or the dependent nature — from its defiled to its purified state through the abandonment of the twofold badness; begun at the first ground and completed at buddhahood, where the consciousnesses become the four wisdoms.
The mindless, non-apprehending knowledge in which the transformation of the basis takes place.

The wisdom that does not construct its object — preparatory, fundamental (the direct realization of suchness) and subsequently obtained; not mere absence of thought; first gained on the path of seeing.

cross_language.form: rnam par mi rtog pa'i ye shes

equivalents.note: Both name a knowing free of conceptual construction; Yogācāra insists it is a cognition of suchness, not the resting of the witness-self Advaita speaks of.

definitions.definition: The pure worldly knowledge obtained after non-conceptual wisdom, which knows dependent things as illusion-like and serves beings.
The meditative non-apprehension of objects, and then of mind, by which the dharmadhātu is apprehended; understanding (parijñā) of the three natures is non-apprehension.
The transformed basis at buddhahood: inconceivable, wholesome, constant, blissful, the liberation-body, the dharma-body of the great sage.
The transformed basis as the liberation attained by arhats as well as buddhas, distinguished from the dharma-body that is the buddhas' alone.

The buddhas' body as the purified dharmadhātu; in the three-body scheme the natural body, basis of the other two; at the Triṃśikā's close, the transformed basis 'called the dharma-body of the great sage'.
The first of the three bodies, the dharmadhātu itself, equal, subtle, the support of the enjoyment and emanation bodies.
The body in which buddhas enjoy the Dharma with assemblies of bodhisattvas in their fields, differing by assemblies, fields, names and forms.
The immeasurable emanations (craftsman, birth, awakening, parinirvāṇa and so on) by which buddhas act for beings.
The unmoving wisdom on which the other three depend: without 'mine', unbounded, ever-present, unconfused about all knowables without facing them; in Faxiang, the transformed eighth consciousness.

cross_language.form: me long lta bu'i ye shes
大圓鏡智 da yuanjing zhi

definitions.definition: The wisdom that sees all beings as equal, abiding in non-abiding peace, with great love and compassion; in Faxiang, the transformed seventh (afflicted) mind.

cross_language.form: mnyam pa nyid kyi ye shes

definitions.definition: The wisdom unobstructed toward all knowables, a treasury of dhāraṇīs and concentrations, that cuts all doubts and rains the Dharma; in Faxiang, the transformed sixth consciousness.

cross_language.form: so sor rtog pa'i ye shes
妙觀察智 miao guancha zhi

literal: wisdom that accomplishes what is to be done

definitions.definition: The wisdom that acts for all beings through countless emanations in all realms; in Faxiang, the transformed five sense-consciousnesses.

cross_language.form: bya ba grub pa'i ye shes

definitions.definition: The nirvāṇa of buddhas, abiding neither in saṃsāra (by wisdom) nor in quiescence (by compassion): the fruit as abandonment.

cross_language.form: mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa

definitions.definition: The first of the five paths: accumulating merit and knowledge through discipline, hearing and reflection; for bodhisattvas, the stage of practice by resolve (adhimukticaryā).

The second path, of the four aids to penetration (heat, peak, patience, supreme mundane quality), in which the yogin realizes that objects are mental speech and mind-only and abandons first the distraction of the grasped, then of the grasper.

The third path: the first supramundane, non-conceptual seeing of suchness free of duality, which is the first ground and the beginning of the transformation of the basis; sixteen moments regarding the four truths.

cross_language.form: 通達位 tongda wei; 見道 jiandao

definitions.definition: The fourth path, through the remaining grounds, cultivating non-conceptual and subsequent wisdom until the diamond-like concentration.
The fifth path, of the one beyond training: the final transformation of the basis, buddhahood.

cross_language.form: mthar phyin pa'i lam; mi slob lam

definitions.definition: The four stages of the path of preparation — heat, peak, patience and supreme mundane quality — which the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra describes as successive stages of seeing objects as mental speech, abiding in mind-only, abandoning the grasped and then the grasper.

cross_language.form: nges par 'byed pa'i cha dang mthun pa

definitions.definition: First aid to penetration: the bodhisattva in concentration no longer sees objects apart from mental speech.
Second aid to penetration: the light of the Dharma is increased by firm vigour.
Third aid to penetration: abiding in mind-only, the distraction of the grasped object is abandoned; also the perfection of patience.
Fourth aid to penetration: only the distraction of the grasper remains, and the immediate concentration is touched.
The concentration immediately preceding the path of seeing, at the end of which the distraction of the grasper ceases.

cross_language.form: bar chad med pa'i ting nge 'dzin

definitions.definition: The final concentration of the path of cultivation, unbreakable by conceptions, followed by the final transformation of the basis and omniscience.

cross_language.form: rdo rje lta bu'i ting nge 'dzin

definitions.definition: One of the ten grounds of the bodhisattva, the first beginning with the transformation of the basis on the path of seeing; the grounds are the antidotes to ten ignorances regarding the dharmadhātu (Madhyāntavibhāga 2.16).
The ten perfections: generosity, discipline, patience, vigour, meditation, wisdom, skill in means, aspiration, power and knowledge, the last four added to the six to match the ten grounds.
The wish for perfect awakening for the sake of others (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.19); its first arising is the bodhisattva's first vow, with awakening and beings' welfare as its two objects.
The generation of the resolve for awakening, the root of the bodhisattva career.
The discipline undertaken by a bodhisattva before a qualified teacher, with its four offences equivalent to defeat and lesser faults (Bodhisattvabhūmi śīla-paṭala; Candragomin's Twenty Verses).

cross_language.form: byang chub sems dpa'i sdom pa

definitions.definition: The bodhisattva's discipline of restraint, of gathering wholesome dharmas, and of acting for beings.
The nature of all dharmas as beyond verbal expression, the object of the knowledge purified of the cognitive obscuration; words refer only to designations.

The nine stages of calm: placing, settling firmly, re-settling, settling closely, taming, calming, calming fully, one-pointing, and concentrating; achieved by six powers and accompanied by four attentions.

Attention, a universal mental factor; in the Śrāvakabhūmi also the four attentions of the nine stages (forced, interrupted, uninterrupted, spontaneous) and the seven attentions leading to the absorptions.
The workability of body and mind that removes badness, arising with calm; one of the eight antidotal formations and a wholesome factor.
The supreme workability of mind reached by purifying absorption, the basis for the higher knowledges.
The totality of the knowable: all conditioned things in the aggregates, all dharmas in elements and bases, all knowables in the truths.
The reality, suchness, of the meditation object, established by four reasonings.
The four reasonings by which the reality of things is established: of dependence, of efficacy (cause and effect), of valid proof, and of the nature of things (dharmatā).
A teaching whose meaning must be drawn out; the Saṃdhinirmocana counts the first and second turnings as surpassable and provisional.
A teaching whose meaning is explicit and final; for the Saṃdhinirmocana, the third, well-distinguished turning.
The first of the afflicted mind's four afflictions: taking the store-consciousness as a self.
Seeing a self, from which comes love for it, thirst for happiness, appropriation and all faults; removed by seeing selflessness.
Ignorance about the self, second affliction of the afflicted mind.
The conceit 'I am', third affliction of the afflicted mind.
Attachment to the self, fourth affliction of the afflicted mind.
A mindless attainment in which the six consciousnesses and the afflicted mind cease, while the store-consciousness continues — one of Yogācāra's reasons for positing the ālaya.
The mindless absorption (and the heaven of non-perceiving gods) in which mental consciousness does not arise.
The moral quality of the store-consciousness and its factors: neither wholesome nor unwholesome and not obscured by afflictions (unlike the afflicted mind, which is obscured-neutral).
The store-consciousness as the ripened result of past action; a new maturation arises when the previous one is exhausted.
The condition by which cognitions of different streams determine each other, explaining intersubjective and karmic effects without external objects.
A higher knowledge which, like knowledge of one's own mind, does not accord with its object because of ignorance — unlike the buddhas'.
Cognition-only in all its aspects, inconceivable except to the buddhas.
Mind is luminous by nature and its defilements are adventitious; hence emptiness is neither defiled nor pure, and only the mind that is dharmatā is luminous by nature.
This mind is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious — so they can be removed by the cultivation of selflessness.
Defilements are adventitious to the luminous mind and therefore removable.
The stains are adventitious; they have no support in the nature of mind and cannot survive the cultivation of their antidote.
In the Triṃśikā's 'self and dharmas', the factors of existence of Abhidharma, which are only figuratively designated on the transformation of consciousness and lack imagined own-nature.
Only a figurative designation on the transformation of consciousness; the afflicted mind mistakes the store-consciousness for it.
A permanent self is refuted: nothing permanent can be causally efficacious; seeing a self is the root of attachment and all faults.
One in whom the store-consciousness, as ālaya, has ceased and the afflicted mind is absent; a disciple-vehicle arhat still has the cognitive obscuration.
Action is volition, whose imprints in the store-consciousness, with those of the twofold grasping, produce future maturations; mental action is the gravest.
Volition, a universal mental factor; in Vasubandhu's Karmasiddhi, action itself.
The twelve fields were taught with a special intention: cognition's seed and its appearance as object are the 'two fields' of each cognition.
In Paramārtha's teaching (and the Shelun school) a ninth, pure consciousness beyond the ālaya, identified with suchness.

notes: Faxiang (Kuiji) rejects a ninth consciousness; amala is for them a name of the purified eighth.

definitions.definition: The position that cognition bears images (ākāra) of its objects; in late Indian debate, that these images are real (satyākāra, Jñānaśrīmitra) or false (alīkākāra, Ratnākaraśānti).
The position that pure cognition is image-free, the appearing images being false superimpositions.
The view that cognition's images are real as cognition (rnam bden pa).
The view that cognition's images are unreal and only image-free luminosity is real (rnam rdzun pa).
